title: When errors are not normal
objectives: Choose a distribution and a link function for counts, proportions and yes or no outcomes.

screens.title: A straight line through defaults
screens.prose: Each dot is one of 300 firms, at its leverage $L$ (debt over assets). It sits at 1 if the firm defaulted within a year, else at 0. 106 defaulted. A straight line through these dots is a default probability that rises with $L$.
screens.question: Drag the ends $A$ and $B$ to where least squares would put the line. It minimises the squared vertical misses.

hints.text: Most low-leverage firms survive, so the line sits near 0 there. The defaults at high $L$ pull it up.
To meet the many 0s on the left and the many 1s on the right, the line gets steep. A steep line starts below 0.
Put $A$ near $-0.2$ and $B$ near $0.96$.

feedback.correct: Least squares gives $\hat p = -0.1988 + 1.1549L$. Its left end is below zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Least squares puts $A$ at about $-0.20$ and $B$ at about $0.96$.

byKey.A: Your left end is too high. Least squares tilts the line to meet the survivors and the defaults. So tilted, it starts below 0.
byKey.B: Your right end is off. At $L = 1$ the least-squares line reaches about 0.96.

explain.text: The dashed line is the least-squares fit, $\hat p = -0.198849 + 1.154923L$. A debt-free firm gets a default probability of $-19.9\%$. No price or reserve can use that number.

screens.title: How many firms get a negative probability
screens.prose: The least-squares line is $\hat p = -0.198849 + 1.154923L$. Below some leverage it predicts a negative default probability.
screens.question: At what leverage does the line cross 0?

hints.text: Set $\hat p = 0$ and solve for $L$.

feedback.correct: $L = 0.1722$. Every firm with less leverage gets a negative probability.

byKey.intercept: You gave the intercept's size. That is where the line sits at $L = 0$, not where it crosses 0.
byKey.one: You solved $\hat p = 1$. That point is past $L = 1$, so no firm here gets a probability above 1.

explain.text: The line crosses 0 at $L = 0.1722$. Of the 300 firms, 68 have less leverage, so 68 fitted values (22.7%) lie outside $[0, 1]$. None lie above 1, because the line reaches 1 only at $L = 1.038$.

screens.title: Bend the line
screens.prose: Now feed the straight line $\eta = b_0 + b_1L$ through $\mu = 1/(1 + e^{-\eta})$. Move both sliders until the curve follows the cloud. Try a very low $b_0$ too.

derive.caption: $\eta = b_0 + b_1L$ runs from {{fixed(b0, 1)}} to {{fixed(b0 + b1, 1)}}. The curve gives {{fixed(100/(1 + exp(-b0)), 1)}}% at $L = 0$.

screens.question: However far you push the sliders, the curve stays between 0 and 1. What does that?

options.text: The function $1/(1 + e^{-\eta})$ that the straight line is fed through
The data, because every outcome is 0 or 1
options.why: The straight line saw the same 0s and 1s and still went below 0. The data alone do not bound the fit.
A small slope only delays the problem: a straight line with any slope leaves $[0, 1]$ somewhere.

feedback.correct: The squashing function maps every $\eta$, however large, into $(0, 1)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Watch what happens to $\eta$ and to the curve as you push $b_0$ down.

explain.text: You just built a **generalised linear model** (GLM). It has a distribution for $Y$ (Bernoulli), a linear predictor $\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1L$ and a link $g(\mu) = \eta$. Here $g(\mu) = \ln\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}$, the logit, and its inverse is your squashing curve.

screens.title: A family and a link for each outcome
screens.prose: Each kind of outcome has its own distribution. Its link maps the mean onto the whole real line, where $\eta$ lives.

rows: A firm defaults within a year
Seconds until a limit order fills

screens.question: Put a family and its usual link against each outcome.

hints.text: A count with no upper limit and a count out of 10 need different families.
Means between 0 and 1 take the logit. Positive means take the log.
Bernoulli and binomial take logit; Poisson and Gamma take log.

feedback.correct: Bernoulli and binomial with the logit; Poisson and Gamma with the log.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the range of each outcome first, then the link that frees its mean.

byKey.norm: A normal family allows negative values and any spread. None of these outcomes can be negative.
byKey.ident: With the identity link the mean is $\eta$ itself, which can go below 0. That is the straight line you dragged.
byKey.pois: A Poisson count has no upper limit. Fills out of 10 cannot exceed 10, so they are binomial.
byKey.bin: Binomial counts stop at a known $n$. Trades in a minute have no such cap, so they are Poisson.

explain.text: The logit sends a mean in $(0, 1)$ to the real line; the log sends a positive mean there. Each pairing is the family's canonical link, except Gamma's, which is usually fitted with the log.

screens.title: The variance function
screens.prose: Each family ties its variance to its mean: $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \phi V(\mu)$, with $\phi = 1$ for Bernoulli and Poisson. A Bernoulli outcome has $V(\mu) = \mu(1 - \mu)$, a Poisson count $\mu$, a Gamma time $\mu^2$.
screens.question: Fill in $V(\mu)$ at each mean.

hints.text: Put each mean into its own family's formula.
Bernoulli: $0.2 \times 0.8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\mu(1 - \mu)$, $\mu$ and $\mu^2$ in turn.

byKey.r0c2: If you wrote 0.2, that is the mean. A Bernoulli variance is $\mu(1 - \mu)$, which is smaller.
byKey.r1c2: If you squared the mean, that is the Gamma rule. A Poisson variance equals its mean.
byKey.r2c2: If you wrote 2, you used the Poisson rule for the Gamma time. A Gamma variance grows with the square of the mean.

explain.text: The variance function is a family's second fingerprint. A Poisson model with mean 4.405 promises a variance of 4.405, which the next screen tests.

screens.title: Does the variance match the mean
screens.prose: A desk counts its limit-order fills on each of 200 days. The mean is 4.405 fills a day and the sample variance is 17.117.

state.caption: 200 trading days of fills on one desk.

screens.question: What is the variance divided by the mean? A Poisson count would give about 1.

hints.text: Divide the variance by the mean.
About 3.89.

feedback.correct: 3.89: the counts spread almost four times as much as a Poisson count would.

byKey.recip: You divided the mean by the variance. Put the variance on top.
byKey.sd: You divided the standard deviation, $\sqrt{17.117} = 4.137$, by the mean. Use the variance.

explain.text: The ratio is $17.117 / 4.405 = 3.89$. The 28 zero days and the long right tail are both too many for a Poisson count. Lesson 5 calls this overdispersion and tests for it.

screens.title: Why not log the counts
screens.prose: Trades per minute are Poisson with mean 2. A colleague says: skip GLMs, take $\ln$ of each count and run ordinary least squares.
screens.question: What is wrong with the plan?

options.text: A zero count has no log, and $\ln(y + 1)$ fits $E[\ln(Y + 1)]$, not $\ln E[Y]$
Nothing: OLS on $\ln y$ is the log link
options.why: The log link models $\ln E[Y]$. Logging each count first models the mean of the logs, a different quantity.

options.text: Nothing that matters, since least squares slopes stay unbiased
options.why: Unbiased for what? Here OLS estimates the slope of $E[\ln(Y + 1)]$, not of $\ln E[Y]$.

hints.text: Look at the shaded bar.
13.5% of minutes have no trades. What is $\ln 0$?
Adding 1 dodges the zero but changes the quantity: $E[\ln(Y + 1)] \neq \ln(E[Y] + 1)$.

feedback.correct: Zeros break the log, and the patch of adding 1 models a different mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check what happens to the zero counts, then to the mean.

byKey.same: You treated logging each count as the log link. The link transforms the mean; the transform logs each observation.
byKey.unbias: You trusted unbiasedness. OLS estimates a slope, but of the wrong curve, and its predictions can be impossible.

explain.text: $P(Y = 0) = e^{-2} = 13.5\%$, and $\ln 0$ does not exist. With the $+1$ patch, $E[\ln(Y + 1)] = 0.9780$ while $\ln(E[Y] + 1) = \ln 3 = 1.0986$. A GLM with a log link models $\ln E[Y]$ directly and keeps the zeros as data.

screens.title: Link the mean, not the data
screens.prose:
For $Y \sim$ Poisson(2), the pmf sum $\sum_y P(Y = y)\ln(y + 1)$ gives 0.9780, and a million simulated draws give 0.9782. But $\ln(E[Y] + 1) = 1.0986$. In general:
$$g(E[Y]) \neq E[g(Y)]$$
A GLM writes $g(\mu) = \eta = \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol\beta$, with $\mu = E[Y]$, so the data stay as they are.
screens.question: A Poisson GLM with a log link fits a straight line to which quantity?

options.why: That is what OLS on $\ln(y + 1)$ fits: the mean of the transformed data.
A straight line in $E[Y]$ is the identity link, which can go negative.

feedback.correct: The link acts on the mean: $\ln E[Y] = \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol\beta$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The link is applied to $\mu = E[Y]$, not to each $y$.

explain.text: Because $g$ is applied to the mean, a zero count is just a small observation. The gap between 0.9780 and 1.0986 is the price of transforming the data instead.

screens.title: Links and variance functions in code
screens.prose: Every GLM routine needs the link, its inverse and the variance function. Write them for NumPy arrays, so one call handles a whole column.
screens.question: Complete the three functions. Raise `ValueError` for a name you do not know.

widget.how: Check runs 14 hidden tests: exact values within $10^{-12}$, arrays rounded to 6 places, and `ValueError` for unknown names. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Each function is a chain of `if name == ...` branches.
Convert the input with `np.asarray(mu, dtype=float)` so lists and numbers both work.
End each function with `raise ValueError(...)` after the known names.

feedback.correct: All three work on arrays and refuse unknown names.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the logit formula and that an unknown name raises `ValueError`.

explain.text: `inverse_link('logit', 0)` is 0.5 because $\eta = 0$ is even odds. These three functions are all that differ between a logistic and a Poisson fit in lesson 4.

screens.title: A default probability a bank can price
screens.prose: A bank lends £1,000,000 to a firm with leverage $L = 0.05$. It expects to lose 45% of the loan if the firm defaults, so expected loss is $\text{PD} \times 0.45 \times \text{£}1{,}000{,}000$. The straight line gives a PD of $-14.1\%$ and an expected loss of $-\text{£}63{,}496$.
screens.question: The logistic GLM fit is $\hat\mu = 1/(1 + e^{-(-5.451164 + 8.690639L)})$. What expected loss does it give, in pounds?

hints.text: First the linear predictor at $L = 0.05$, then the inverse logit, then the loss.

feedback.correct: £2,962: a small, positive loss that can go into a price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the PD from the logistic curve, then multiply by 0.45 and the loan.

byKey.line: That is the straight line's answer. A negative expected loss would say the loan earns money from a default.
byKey.nolgd: You left out the 45% loss given default. Only 45% of the loan is lost in a default.

explain.text: The GLM gives PD $= 0.658\%$ and an expected loss of £2,962. The straight line gave $-\text{£}63{,}496$, which no pricing sum can use. A model whose mean lives in $(0, 1)$ is a requirement, not a nicety.

ideas: A straight line fitted to 0/1 outcomes predicts impossible probabilities: 68 of 300 firms got a negative one.
A GLM has three parts: a family for $Y$, a linear predictor $\eta = \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol\beta$ and a link $g(\mu) = \eta$.
Each family has a variance function: $\mu(1 - \mu)$ for Bernoulli, $\mu$ for Poisson, $\mu^2$ for Gamma.

formula.name: A generalised linear model
formula.note: Logit for 0/1 and proportions, log for counts and positive times.

summary.trap: Logging the counts and running OLS breaks on zeros and models $E[\ln(Y + 1)]$, not $\ln E[Y]$.

quiz.prose: A market maker records how many of its quotes are cancelled in each second.
quiz.question: Which family and link suit this outcome?

options.why: A binomial needs a fixed number of trials. Cancels per second have no cap.
A normal model can predict negative counts and assumes a constant variance.
A Gamma variable is continuous and positive. A count of 0 is impossible for it.

feedback.correct: A count per interval with no cap: Poisson, log link.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The outcome is a count with no upper limit.

explain.text: A count per second is Poisson, and the log link keeps its mean positive.

quiz.prose: In one sector all 5 firms with leverage above 0.95 defaulted. Fitted alone, that group's default share is $5/5 = 1$.
quiz.question: What logit does a fitted share of 1 give?

options.text: It is infinite, so no finite coefficient fits that group

options.why: A logit of 0 is a share of 0.5, even odds.
You applied the identity link. $\ln\frac{1}{1 - 1}$ divides by zero.

explain.text: $\ln\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}$ grows without bound as $\mu \to 1$. A group whose outcomes are all 1 pushes its coefficient to infinity; lesson 4 meets this as separation.

quiz.question: What variance does the Bernoulli family give it?

byKey.mu: You gave the mean. A Bernoulli variance is $\mu(1 - \mu)$.
byKey.sq: You squared the mean. That is the Gamma rule.

explain.text: $V(0.3) = 0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21$, largest at $\mu = 0.5$ and small near 0 and 1.

quiz.prose: A colleague keeps the straight line for defaults: "least squares on 0/1 data is still unbiased for the slope".
quiz.question: What is the problem the claim ignores?

options.text: Its fitted probabilities leave $[0, 1]$: 68 of our 300 firms got a negative one
The slope is biased towards zero
options.why: The slope estimates the straight line's slope without bias. The trouble is that the probability is not a straight line.

options.text: Least squares cannot give a confidence interval
options.why: It can give one; the problem is what the fitted values say.

feedback.correct: The fitted values are not probabilities.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the fitted values, not the slope.

explain.text: A straight line gave 68 of 300 firms a negative PD. Unbiasedness of a slope does not rescue predictions that cannot be priced.
